objective.offer: run the CLI locally, no account

hero.headline: Thirty seconds to find out whether this is useful.
hero.subhead: `npx @attestci/cli scan .` reads your source and prints what it found. No account, no signup, nothing transmitted. If the findings are not interesting, you have lost thirty seconds and you can close the tab.

proofLine.text: On three well-known Next.js repositories it found 8, 16 and 54 things — and two bugs in itself, which are published.

hero.trustLine: MIT licensed. Needs `contents: read`, plus `pull-requests: write` only if you want the comment.

sections.heading: The whole setup
sections.code:
name: attest
on: pull_request

permissions:
  contents: read
  pull-requests: write

jobs:
  attest:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0     # so the base commit can be scanned for comparison
      - uses: attest-ci/attest-action@v1
sections.caption: `fail-on-new-only` is on by default, so an existing codebase adopts the check without having to fix everything first. A check that goes red on day one gets removed on day two.

sections.heading: What lands on the pull request
sections.code:
Accessibility conformance changed
checkout/PaymentForm: 3 new WCAG 2.1 AA violations (label association, focus order)

Privacy boundary changed
customer_profile: session-private → reachable from shared cache

Client impact
+18 KB startup JavaScript, one new sequential server fetch
sections.caption: One comment, edited in place on each push. Findings are fingerprinted without line numbers, so adding an import at the top of a file does not report the ten findings below it as new.

sections.heading: The kind of thing it finds
sections.caption: `'use client'` marks a boundary, not a file. Everything a client module imports also ships, so an ordinary helper becomes browser code and the environment variable it reads becomes `undefined` there — silently. ESLint reads one file at a time and cannot answer this.

sections.heading: What runs, and what each layer needs
columns: Runs in the Action by default
rows: A running app and a browser
sections.note: A layer that could not run is reported as **did not run**, never as clean. If you do not pass URLs, the comment says the runtime accessibility checks were skipped and why.

sections.heading: Two false positives, published
body: Pointed at real repositories for the first time, this scanner produced two false positives within an hour. Neither had been caught by any test.

It followed type-only imports, making a `lib/types.ts` look like it dragged a database layer into the browser — critical severity, on correct code. And it matched JSX tags case-insensitively, so `<Input>` was treated as `<input>`, reporting 106 phantom missing labels in one repository.
Both fixed, both with regression fixtures, both written up with before-and-after counts. A tool whose false positives you only discover yourself is a tool you should not install.

sections.heading: What it does not do
rows: Whether an image has a text alternative
Whether the alt text is correct
Whether a form control can be labelled at all
Pages you do not, and states you never navigated to
Vue, Svelte, Rails, PDFs, video captions, native apps
sections.note: Automated tooling can evaluate roughly a quarter to a third of WCAG 2.1 success criteria. It does not make you compliant, and no tool can. This is not legal advice.

sections.heading: Price
rows: Free — CLI, all 30 rules, Action, PR comment, SARIF, badge
Solo — hosted history for one repository
Team — ten repositories, policy, signed evidence export
sections.note: The hosted service is written and tested but is **not yet available**. The free tier is the whole tool and does not become a trial later.

sections.heading: Try it before you install anything
sections.body: The CLI needs no account and no permissions. Run it on a repository where you would recognise a wrong answer, then decide whether the Action is worth adding.
